live_plab_copy.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with increasing fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. His blood tests show a microcytic anaemia. Which test is most useful for assessing his iron stores?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Ferritin reflects body iron stores and is usually low in iron-deficiency anaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Serum bilirubin: May help assess haemolysis but does not measure iron stores. B. Serum calcium: Assesses calcium metabolism, not iron status. D. Serum folate: Assesses folate deficiency. E. Serum vitamin B12: Assesses B12 deficiency, which usually causes macrocytosis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, but ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so a normal level does not exclude it during inflammation; iron deficiency in a man needs GI investigation.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Fatigue and exertional breathlessness ↓ Microcytic anaemia ↓ Iron deficiency most likely ↓ Ferritin reflects iron stores ↓ Serum ferritin
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, serum vitamin B12 — part of a routine anaemia screen, but B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and says nothing about iron stores.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Microcytic anaemia: check ferritin; iron deficiency in a man needs GI investigation.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 23-year-old woman has fatigue and recurrent abdominal pain. Blood tests show microcytic anaemia. Which additional finding would support iron deficiency rather than thalassaemia trait?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Ferritin is usually preserved in thalassaemia trait. C. A family history supports an inherited haemoglobin disorder. D. Lifelong asymptomatic microcytosis is more suggestive of thalassaemia trait. E. A relatively high red-cell count can occur in thalassaemia trait.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, normal ferritin — ferritin is the right test, but a normal result points away from iron deficiency and towards thalassaemia trait.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Microcytosis: low ferritin = iron deficiency; normal ferritin = consider thalassaemia trait.

A patient has anaemia, jaundice and a raised reticulocyte count.

Which process should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Anaemia with jaundice (unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia) and a raised reticulocyte count indicates increased red cell destruction with a compensatory marrow response, typical of haemolysis.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, chronic blood loss only — a common cause of anaemia, but it leads to iron deficiency without jaundice.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Anaemia plus jaundice plus reticulocytosis means haemolysis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 67-year-old man taking warfarin develops prolonged bleeding after a minor injury. Which laboratory test is routinely used to monitor the anticoagulant effect of warfarin?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Warfarin therapy is monitored using the international normalised ratio (INR), which reflects its effect on the extrinsic/common coagulation pathway.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Fibrinogen: Does not routinely measure warfarin anticoagulation. C. Bleeding time: Is not routinely used to monitor warfarin. D. APTT: Is primarily used to monitor unfractionated heparin. E. Platelet count: Measures platelet number rather than warfarin effect.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Warfarin is monitored by the INR, a standardised prothrombin time; the target range depends on the indication, and a raised INR increases bleeding risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors ↓ Prolongs the prothrombin time ↓ Standardised as the INR ↓ INR
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, APTT — a clotting test that sounds right for anticoagulants, but APTT is used for unfractionated heparin; warfarin is monitored by the INR.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Warfarin: INR. Unfractionated heparin: APTT.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 70-year-old man has persistent back pain and is diagnosed with multiple myeloma.

Which blood abnormality is commonly associated with this condition?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Myeloma can cause increased bone resorption and hypercalcaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Marrow infiltration can cause cytopenias, but isolated severe neutropenia is not the characteristic finding. B. Paraprotein production commonly increases serum protein. C. Inflammatory markers are often raised rather than characteristically low. E. Hypoglycaemia is not a typical feature.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Myeloma features are summarised as CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions; persistent bone pain in an older adult should prompt protein electrophoresis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Myeloma is CRAB: calcium high, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Calcium may be raised in myeloma but does not detect a paraprotein. C. A skeletal survey detects lytic lesions, not a paraprotein. D. ESR may be raised but is non-specific. E. ALP is typically normal in myeloma and does not detect a paraprotein.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, skeletal survey — part of the myeloma work-up and tempting, but it shows lytic bone lesions; only electrophoresis detects the monoclonal paraprotein itself.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Detect a paraprotein with protein electrophoresis and free light chains.

A patient with severe malabsorption develops unexpected bleeding and a prolonged clotting time.

Which vitamin deficiency may be responsible?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Vitamin K is required for synthesis of several clotting factors, so deficiency can cause bleeding and prolonged clotting times.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not coagulopathy. B. live_plab_copy.takeaway: Malabsorption with bleeding and prolonged PT: think vitamin K deficiency.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Bleeding with a normal platelet count on aspirin reflects impaired platelet function.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops acute blood loss after trauma. Initially, which type of anaemia is most likely?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Megaloblastic anaemia is usually due to impaired DNA synthesis. C. Sideroblastic anaemia is a different disorder of haem synthesis. D. Microcytosis develops with iron deficiency over time. E. Macrocytosis is associated with conditions such as B12/folate deficiency.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Acute blood loss after trauma ↓ Whole blood lost, so cells unchanged ↓ No time for iron stores to run down ↓ Remaining red cells are normal-sized ↓ Normocytic anaemia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, microcytic anaemia — blood loss is a classic cause of microcytosis, but only chronic loss causing iron deficiency, not an acute bleed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Acute haemorrhage causes normocytic anaemia; chronic loss causes microcytosis.

A patient is about to receive a blood transfusion.

Which principle is essential?

options.A: Confirm patient identity and compatibility at the bedside
options.B: Confirm identity using the bed number and the prescription chart

options.D: Rely on the patient stating their name if they are well known

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Confirm patient identity and compatibility at the bedside

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, hereditary spherocytosis — also an inherited haemolytic anaemia, but it is not specifically triggered by fava beans or oxidant stress.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Haemolysis after fava beans or oxidant drugs = G6PD deficiency.

akt_source.stem: A 10-year-old boy develops jaundice and dark urine after eating fava beans. Blood tests show evidence of haemolysis. Which inherited disorder is most likely?
akt_source.why_correct: Oxidative stress from fava beans can precipitate acute haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency.
akt_source.why_wrong: B. Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis but is not specifically triggered by oxidative drugs or fava beans. C. Von Willebrand disease causes abnormal bleeding. D. Haemophilia causes bleeding rather than haemolysis. E. Thalassaemia trait is usually asymptomatic or causes mild microcytosis rather than an acute oxidative haemolytic crisis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 35-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful swollen joints and a family history of sickle cell disease. Which inherited condition should be considered if she has chronic haemolytic anaemia?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder that can cause chronic haemolysis and episodic painful crises.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenia primarily affects platelets. B. Aplastic anaemia causes bone-marrow failure. C. Iron deficiency does not cause recurrent vaso-occlusive crises. D. B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia and neurological features.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobinopathy causing chronic haemolytic anaemia and painful vaso-occlusive crises, often affecting bones and joints.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Family history of sickle cell disease ↓ Recurrent painful episodes ↓ Chronic haemolytic anaemia ↓ Inherited haemoglobin disorder ↓ Sickle cell disease
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, iron-deficiency anaemia — the commonest anaemia overall, but it is not inherited, not haemolytic and causes no painful crises.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Haemolysis, painful crises and a family history point to sickle cell disease.
